verses.text: The elder to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth.
Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be healthy, even as your soul prospers.
For I rejoiced greatly, when brothers came and testified about your truth, even as you walk in truth.
I have no greater joy than this, to hear about my children walking in truth.
Beloved, you do a faithful work in whatever you accomplish for those who are brothers and strangers.
They have testified about your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them forward on their journey in a way worthy of God,
because for the sake of the Name they went out, taking nothing from the Gentiles.
We therefore ought to receive such, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say.

Therefore if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words. Not content with this, neither does he himself receive the brothers, and those who would, he forbids and throws out of the assembly.
Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God.
Demetrius has the testimony of all, and of the truth itself; yes, we also testify, and you know that our testimony is true.
I had many things to write to you, but I am unwilling to write to you with ink and pen;
but I hope to see you soon, and we will speak face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.

footnotes.content: John calls himself simply 'the elder'—not claiming authority, just offering love that's been tested and held. He writes to Gaius as 'beloved,' the word he used for his closest disciple. This is how truth binds people: not through titles, but through a love that's real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A simple prayer—that Gaius would prosper and be well, as his soul prospers. John knows that when the inner life is nourished in Christ, a person can flourish in every way. He's not asking for riches, but for wholeness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Brothers have come bringing good news of Gaius's faithfulness. John rejoices—not in gossip, but in the testimony that someone is walking honestly with God. This is the news that matters most: that a person is living what they believe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John uses the language of fatherhood: his 'children' in the faith. There is no greater joy than to see those you've poured into choosing the narrow way, staying true. This is what pastors and grandparents know: the deepest satisfaction is in others' faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaius shows faithful work toward 'brothers and strangers'—no distinction. This is the mark of real love: it doesn't calculate or check credentials. He serves the Lord's people not because he owes them, but because they belong to his Father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The whole assembly has noticed Gaius's hospitality and spoken well of him. John urges him to continue, to send travelers forward 'in a way worthy of God.' Real hospitality isn't just shelter—it's recognizing Christ in the stranger and honoring Him through them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These travelers went out for the sake of Jesus' Name and took nothing from outsiders. They lived by faith, dependent on God's people to sustain them. This is a picture of radical trust—going where the Lord calls, not where the pay is sure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To receive such faithful workers is to become a 'fellow worker for the truth.' Hospitality isn't passive kindness—it's partnership in the gospel. When you welcome Christ's ambassadors, you join the work they're doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Diotrephes loves to be first—a name John sets against this brightness. He rejects John's instruction, perhaps from wounded pride or hunger for control. This is how darkness works in a congregation: one person's need to dominate can poison the whole body.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Diotrephes spreads slander, refuses to receive brothers, and throws out those who do. His tyranny is built on lies and isolation—separating people from one another so none dare challenge him. John won't ignore this: he will come and expose it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John calls Gaius back to the ancient truth: 'Don't imitate evil, but good.' Those who do good belong to God; those who do evil haven't truly known Him. A life reveals what you worship. Keep watching your own heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Demetrius stands in sharp contrast to Diotrephes—'all' testify to his goodness, and truth itself speaks for him. John adds his own witness. When someone walks in integrity, they need no defense; their life defends them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John has much more to say, but he won't spill it all onto paper. There are limits to what ink can carry—some things demand the warmth of a face, the sound of a voice, the presence of a person. Some truths must be spoken, not written.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in John's longing: 'I hope to see you soon, and we will speak face to face.' In our age of screens and distance, the apostle's yearning reminds us that presence matters—true fellowship lives in the room, in the time we give each other. The peace he offers is rooted in that longed-for meeting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
